utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, everyone. I would like to ask the registrar to call the case first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-96-23/2-PT, the Prosecutor versus Radovan Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I would like to have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. My name is Jan Wubben, senior trial attorney for the Prosecution, together with co-counsel Manoj Sachdeva, and our case manager, Djurdja Mirkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I am attorney-at-law Milenko Radovic, from Foca, Defence counsel for Mr. Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Radovic. Mr. Stankovic, are you able to hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. El Mahdi, I can hear you. Despite the fact that my hearing isn't the best, but it is obvious that you do not wish to hear me. This is why I sincerely hope that you will not be able to cut me off at today's conference as was done on two previous occasions. And I hope --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stankovic, listen. Mr. Stankovic -- Mr. Stankovic, you have to listen to me when I talk. This is the golden rule that applies here. And a Judge will never let such disorder happen in a courtroom. There is a rule that we have to -- all of us to follow. If -- listen to me. Listen to me. Listen to me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do not deny me my right to speak pursuant to Rule 65 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Listen to me. You will have the opportunity, but when I ask you a question, you have to answer that question. I'm asking you whether you -- listen to me. You hear me in a language you understand and the only answer you can give is yes or no, Mr. Stankovic. We are not going to start like this, because you're behaving in a very provocative manner, and I am here to fulfil my role to serve justice. Now at least I find that you can hear me in a language you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not here to provide yes or no answers to your questions. You asked me and I gave you an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stankovic, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is exactly what happened on two previous Status Conferences. You left the courtroom refusing to hear me out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stankovic, Mr. Stankovic, that's enough.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- to take opportunity to use my right pursuant to Rule 65 and I hope that you will grant me ten minutes of your valuable time today to allow me to say what I have on my mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's enough. That's enough, Mr. Stankovic. I have to remind you that I will not tolerate some comments. I am not here to be lectured. I have to lecture you here. During the last Status Conference, I asked the Defence to give me their position about a specific matter, the following matter: It was the matter of alibi, of the alibi. I have received a brief that was drawn up, as far as I understand, by Mr. Stankovic himself. It was filed with the Registrar on the 10th of September. In that brief, he states that -- or rather, there is a contradiction in the Rules of the Tribunal, there is a contradiction between Rule 65 ter and Rule 67. I would like to point out to the parties the following: I would like to draw their attention to the French language of Rule 67 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. If we look at the English version of Rule 67, we read, in English: [In English] "The Defence shall notify the Prosecutor of its intent to offer the defence of alibi, in which case the notification shall specify the places or places at which the accused claims to have been present," et cetera. [Interpretation] Whereas if we look at the Rule in French, it says: "The Defence informs the Prosecutor that it is in its intention to invoke, that it intends to invoke." And it's not exactly the equivalent of the language in English. "The Defence shall notify." There is a difference. Furthermore, if we look at the Rule itself in English, we read the following, and I quote: [In English] "The defence of alibi in which case the notification shall specify," et cetera. [Interpretation] In French, when we look at the language of the Rule, we find that it's different, because we read the following: "The defence of alibi, with an indication of the location or specific locations where the accused says that he was at the time of the alleged crime." So I would like to draw the attention of the parties to this difference in the language between the French Rule and the English Rule. When we look at the English Rule, it has a mandatory quality that derives from the use of the verb "shall" in the Rule, whereas if we look at the French Rule, we don't find that element of that quality in the Rule as it is in French. However, the Prosecutor still has to be in a position to present his case. We are faced with a situation where the Defence tells us: Well, I reserve the possibility of setting out my defence of alibi when the time comes to do so. Whereas the Prosecution is saying: Well, in order to be able to prepare my case properly, I need to know what is the nature of the defence of alibi. I believe that the solution is quite clear-cut. If we think back of what is to be found in the pre-trial briefs submitted by Defence counsel and by Mr. Stankovic himself, then we will see that very clearly this alibi consists in the following: During 90 per cent of the time making up the time period in question, or the relevant time period, Mr. Stankovic says that he was at the front, he was fighting. Furthermore, the Defence says, and Mr. Stankovic asserts, that he went to the house, to the house we all know about, he went to that house twice, and he went there on a mission, in order to solve a number of security-related problems. Therefore, I imagine that his defence of alibi is based on a number of elements, not necessarily on witnesses but maybe on producing a military logs or administrative logs that could show that indeed he had been assigned one or several missions during the relevant period, as well as the missions he had to conduct at the house we all know about, we are all familiar with. At this stage, I believe that the Defence, if it does not have the material necessary to support the defence of alibi, I believe that the Defence has the right not to go further to reveal the information before the beginning of the trial, before the beginning of the Prosecution case, or as soon as the information becomes available to the Defence. So that was for the defence of alibi. Now let me move on to another issue. The briefs that were submitted and that set out or reveal information that is considered to be protected information, i.e., the identity of some witnesses or of some victims. This is a very serious matter, and I must say about this matter that the Registry has done its work perfectly because the Registry has filed these briefs confidentially, although the briefs had been submitted confidentially, so as to limit the potential damage. And I would like to ask Mr. Radovic to make sure that when briefs are submitted by the Defence, these briefs should comply with the protective measures that are in place. Now I'm turning to the Prosecution. If I understand correctly, you have completed -- you have your list of witnesses. Is it a final list of witnesses? Have you been able to make an estimate of the time necessary to hear each witness, in order to be able to assess -- to give an assessment of the presentation of your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we have not prepared this issue, as we are now in the stage of filing and proceeding on the 11 bis-ing of the case, so at the very moment I can't confirm to you whether or not it's a final list. I know we have the list, and we are of course still aiming for better witnesses, and to that extent, we have also to deal with this 11 bis motion we filed. In the meanwhile, we rather focus on the outcome of the 11 bis to still be decided by the Trial Chamber. Then, further go into the scheduling of witnesses or the number of witnesses. If Your Honour wants a notification in that regard, we are willing, of course, to file that as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you very much. But I believe that I am in charge of the preparation of this case before this Tribunal, and it is my duty to move ahead in the preparation of the case until we receive a different order, a different instruction. I can't wait for your motion to be decided upon, your 11 bis motion to be decided upon. This does not concern me. It's not within my competence. Therefore, I hope that you will be able to submit information about this matter. If you have that information now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I have that information now. We project 13 witnesses, and in total, 50 hours. But if you ask me: Is this your final number of witnesses? It may be some three more added to it. We don't know at this very stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if you say 13 witnesses, if I understand properly, there will -- it's minus two or plus two. Well, it's around 15 witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as for the number of hours, it's 50 hours. Is that it, 50 hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. It's 50 hours, and I refer, of course, to our pre-trial brief and annexes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. I just wanted to make sure that I understood properly. Thank you very much. Now I'm turning to the Defence. Mr. Radovic, is there any issue you would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on the 21st of September, 2004, the Prosecution submitted a motion pursuant to Rule 11 bis to have the indictment against Mr. Stankovic referred to Bosnia and Herzegovina, to the state court there, to the court for war crimes. In view of that, I would like to state the following: The Defence does not wish to go into details when denying the allegations of the Prosecution. We will do that in our written submissions. However, it is our duty to state here that, in our view, this motion represents the violation of the basic principles contained in the Statute of this Tribunal. Pursuant to Article 21(4)(c) of the Statute, the accused has a right to have a fair trial without any delay, without unnecessary delay. So far, the Defence has stated, on a number of occasions, that we were prepared for the trial. We stated this six months ago. If the motion of the Prosecution were to be granted, if this case indeed is referred to the state court in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this Court was established at a much later date, after Mr. Stankovic surrendered to the authorities and was brought here to the Detention Unit of the UN, this would constitute a violation of the constitution of Republika Srpska, which has been recognised as an entity and its right to have its constitutional order has been recognised as well. The constitution of Republika Srpska bans the extradition of its citizens to other states where they are to stand trial. This motion was submitted to the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is a sort of an international court, because among their composition, they are two international judges and one judge from Bosnia and Herzegovina. In a sovereign state such as Bosnia and Herzegovina, foreigners cannot serve as judges. Such a court, the way it was established, and as I've already stated, represents some kind of an international court, which was not established by the United Nations or at a diplomatic conference, which is the only proper way to establish international courts. Therefore, such a court would have no competence to put Mr. Stankovic on trial. In accordance with Article 9 of the Statute, the parallel jurisdiction is given to national courts, so that if the Chamber grants this motion to refer the case against Mr. Stankovic to national courts in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the only competent court to mount a trial against Mr. Stankovic would be the court with subject matter jurisdiction in Republika Srpska, which would be the district court in Trebinje. The district court in Trebinje has subject matter jurisdiction and is competent to conduct a trial against Mr. Stankovic, especially bearing in mind that the acts and conduct of Mr. Stankovic, pursuant to the indictment of this Tribunal, were carried out in the territory of the former municipality Miljevina, which is currently called the local commune of Miljevina, and this is located in the territory which falls under the jurisdiction of the district court in Trebinje in Republika Srpska. Pursuant to the Law on Criminal Procedure in force in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Republika Srpska, the court which is located in the territory where the crime was committed has territorial jurisdiction over the case. In view of the fact that Mr. Stankovic is charged with committing crimes in the territory of Miljevina, in order to mount a trial against him, the only court with proper competence is the court of Republika Srpska, and as I've already stated, the district court in Trebinje. Rule 11 bis sets forth that, in certain cases, the case may be referred also to the authorities of the government on the territory of which the crime was committed. And under subparagraph 2, it says that it can also be referred to the country in which the accused was arrested, and under subparagraph 3, it says to the country having jurisdiction and being willing and adequately prepared to accept such a case. All of these prerequisites indicate that in order to put Mr. Stankovic on trial in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the only court with proper competencies and jurisdiction would be the district court in Trebinje in Republika Srpska. Here are the reasons for that: It is on the territory of this court that the crimes were allegedly committed, on the territory of this court Mr. Stankovic surrendered himself. This court is located in Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state in the entity of Republika Srpska. And this is an entity which would take upon itself to organise a trial against Mr. Stankovic. What represents an impediment for the Tribunal to rule to send this case for further action to the national court in Bosnia and Herzegovina, to the court for war crimes, is the fact that Mr. Stankovic has spent the last two and a half years in the Detention Unit of this court, pursuant to the request of the Tribunal, that we have reached quite a substantial phase in this case, that pre-trial briefs have been filed and we are ready for trial. We are waiting for the trial for the scheduled. And the trial before this Tribunal would take no more than two months. If this case is referred to the authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Stankovic would wait for his trial for another seven to eight months, at a minimum. Because not all regulations are in place, the regulations which relate to the case before the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, with the war crimes court. As far as I know, there are no conditions, even at a minimum level, to keep an accused in detention, and not even all judges have been elected. In view of the fact that the accused has a right to trial without any delay, the Defence hereby requests the Chamber to schedule a trial, to commence a trial, one phase of which has already been completed. Any other ruling would represent violation of Mr. Stankovic's right to have a fair trial, which is a right that he, as an accused, has. If we do schedule a trial at today's Status Conference, the Defence will continue to comply with all of its obligations stated in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Otherwise, Defence requests that you, Your Honour, as Pre-Trial Judge, suspend all of your previous rulings until the ruling pursuant to the 11 bis request of the Prosecution is handed down. The Defence points out that Rules regulating the procedure, in accordance with the current laws in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in Republika Srpska are not identical to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence here at this Tribunal. Therefore, Defence does not wish to file motions that have not been regulated by national laws, because that would further complicate Mr. Stankovic's position before national courts. The legal regulations of Bosnia and Herzegovina, among others, do not mandate that the Defence has to inform the Prosecution of its intention to use the defence of alibi before the Prosecution starts with its case. Therefore, the Defence has not submitted its written motion to the Chamber until now, stating that we intend to use the defence of alibi, where we would indicate the locations where the Defence claims that Mr. Stankovic was at the time when the crimes he's charged with were allegedly committed. We would also indicate names and addresses of witnesses and any other information we intend to use to support the defence of alibi of Mr. Stankovic as provided by Rule 67(ii)(a). Should you need any further clarification, I'm ready to provide it, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Radovic. I would like to say the following: First, I'm the Pre-Trial Judge in this case, and I'm doing this, I'm doing my job, until further notice. You mentioned the issue of the possible referral of the case to another jurisdiction, to another national jurisdiction, pursuant to Rule 11 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. A Chamber was set up within the Tribunal to rule on the motion submitted for that purpose, but as far as I'm concerned, until further notice, that is to say, until a ruling has been handed down about this motion, I am pursuing my work as a Pre-Trial Judge in this case before this Tribunal. That is why I have made a point of explaining very clearly what I understand from your briefs, from your brief, first of all, of the 21st of June, as well as from the three other briefs submitted by Mr. Stankovic himself on the 15th of July, on the 4th of August, and on the 10th of September. I have been able to understand the nature of your defence case, of your defence of alibi. I've been able to understand what it's all about. And I would like to repeat it, but you can correct me if I'm wrong. What you say is that during 90 per cent of the relevant period of time, Mr. Stankovic was not on the scene; he was fighting at the front, on the front line; and he only went twice, on a mission, in front of the house we are all familiar with. Therefore, I do not see where the problem is when it comes to the defence of alibi. Similarly, I don't see any point in delaying the advancement of the case before this Tribunal. If the case is ready for trial, then I will draw up my report accordingly and fulfil my mission and my duties, regardless of any other motion that do not seem relevant to me. Because I'm not supposed to know anything about these other motions, because these motions are under consideration by a special Trial Chamber, a Trial Chamber that was set up to rule on these motions. Therefore, we do not need to have any more information from you. You said that you were ready to start the trial. I believe that you fully answered the Prosecution by submitting four briefs, one you submitted yourself and three briefs that were drawn up and submitted by Mr. Stankovic himself. However, I'd like to draw your attention to one point. Normally, any accused who is presumed innocent until proven guilty has the possibility of defending himself. But if an accused has Defence counsel, then this should be -- everything should be channelled through the Defence counsel. Because I found out that in the briefs, there was information that could contravene protective measures that had been granted to witnesses and victims. When I saw that, then I asked myself the question whether you were aware of that, whether you had had the opportunity to read these briefs before they were submitted. I was informed by the Senior Legal Officer, who organised a conference with you yesterday, I was informed, therefore, by him that you were not aware of these briefs before they were submitted and filed by the Registry. I would like this to be an exception to the rule, to have been an exception to the rule, and I would like everything, all submissions, to be channelled through you. In one of the briefs, Mr. Stankovic said that he wanted to take the floor and to speak for ten minutes. I am in favour of granting him that time; however, I would like to stress the following for him: To draw his attention to a sentence from his brief dated 10th of September, 2004, the following sentence. I quote in English: [In English] "You cannot force me to confess to something that I personally have not done." End of quote. [Interpretation] I'm surprised, to say the least. I'm surprised to see that something like this could be written to a Judge, furthermore, an international Judge, a professional Judge, a Judge who took an oath, who took the oath to accomplish his duty in full impartiality. Therefore, I believe that this was a slip of the tongue on your part and that you never intentionally or never -- anyone would intentionally write this sentence to a Tribunal. This being said, Mr. Stankovic, you have the floor for ten minutes. I'm all ears.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. El Mahdi, when I address you, I address everyone, including yourself, the Prosecution, and the Registry. You all represent an institution, as far as I'm concerned. Furthermore, I wish to say something concerning the lies and fabrications of Muslim intelligence service AID and their witnesses. As far as they're concerned, I don't care whether I will be tried by this perverse Tribunal in The Hague or by the Dzamahirija courts in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I don't care, because my conscious is clear. One is certain, which is that I will use facts to defend myself from your fabrications and lies, which are based on false testimonies of witnesses used by Prosecution. They have no valid evidence. They just bring here 50, 60 women, Muslims, who testify here about something that actually never took place. But let's leave that aside. Let's leave that for the trial. You can do what you like. But here at stake is my own honour, the honour of my family, the honour of my people, and I will defend it to the end. I'm very proud that by birth I am a Serb, an Orthodox believer. This is a great honour. You cannot imagine what a great honour it is. Had you had any facts that you could use at the trial, you would have started this trial. But, however, I've been waiting here for three years for the trial to start. You mostly prosecute Serbs; then you have a small fraction of Croats and Muslims that you put on trial; and then perhaps some Albanians, just as a spice. You use them to spice your proceedings here. Now that was not enough for you, and you're sending me back to Bosnia to be prosecuted by Ustasha and Dzamahirija courts. You accused me falsely for four crimes, and I will prove my innocence. I've been in prison here for three years without knowing what the charges against me are. You yourself, Mr. El Mahdi, stated on one of the previous conferences that you did not know what the charges against me were. During this entire period, the Prosecution unfolded several scenarios, fabrications, all under direction of your bosses, NATO, the United States, in order to conceal crimes committed against Yugoslavia by NATO and the international community, starting from 1991. NATO and America destroyed Yugoslavia. Yugoslavia, prior to that, was European Union, a model of a European Union country. Now you are lecturing us as to how we enter those international integrations, NATO and so on. We had European Union even before the European Union was established, and our country was a mini European Union. Although you depicted me in the media as the greatest war criminal and you prepared a verdict against me in advance, despite of all that, I will prove contrary. The principle that everybody is the innocent until proven guilty does not hold here. You act completely contrary to that principle. You hold me guilty and the charges of the Prosecution are considered to be proven in advance. We will not provide the information you require pursuant to Rule 67. We will provide it pursuant to Rule 65. So after the Prosecution has completed its case and before the Defence commences its case, this is when we will supply this information. Various things were done to me until now. However, none of that worked, because my dignity, the dignity of my family, the dignity of Serbian people, will never be for sale and has never been for sale. This is something that I count on, that is considered sacred for me. I'm a Serb, and I'm very proud that I have given a contribution in the fight of Serbian people against Ustasha and Mujahedin paramilitary formations. Now that you have seen what you have done, and when you refuse to acknowledge that all of these accusations were false, you have decided to send me to Bosnia and Herzegovina, to that Dzamahirija Mujahedin system that will put me on trial. They have no right to put anyone on trial, let alone me, until they resolve the issue of the Serbs that were expelled, at least from Sarajevo, over 10.000 Serbs were liquidated in Sarajevo alone, and you wish to put me on trial in Sarajevo. These people, civilians, Serbs, were expelled from their apartments in Sarajevo, and over 10.000 Serbs in Sarajevo were killed so that others could get their apartments. And on top of that, you wish to put me on trial in former barracks, Viktor Bubanj. This was a camp, an internment camp for Serbs, where thousands and thousands of Serb civilians from Sarajevo were killed. And you turned that notorious camp into a court where, once again, Serbs would be put on trial. So you turn a camp for Serbs into a court for Serbs, and this is how you conceal the crimes that Mujahedin committed against Serbian people. This is indeed a cynicism. You, Mr. El Mahdi, should be aware of the fact that I cannot give you any compliments here, because you are not keeping me in detention for three years because of compliments. You have kept me for three years here without knowing yourself or telling anyone else what were the charges against me. That's all I have to say. Thank you for today's kindness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Stankovic. I should like to draw your attention to the fact that it's not possible to compliment a Tribunal. This goes against any ethical principle. In the same way that you cannot criticise a Tribunal, in the same way, you cannot express compliments or extend compliments to a Tribunal. Now this being said, I have to repeat what I said at the beginning. I am here to make sure that the preparation of the trial be accomplished properly, in the best possible conditions. I understand from the Prosecution that they are ready for trial. They are ready -- the Prosecution is ready to start the trial, with, of course, the caveat of the motion submitted by the Prosecution under Rule 11 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. I've also noted that the Defence believes it is ready to start the trial. Based on what I said about the defence of alibi, I believe that there is no problem regarding that matter. If there is indeed a contradiction between the two versions of the Rules, the French and the English version, that both have the same power within the Tribunal, then I will accept, I will go for the version of the Rules that is in favour of the Defence. And if we take the Rule in French, then the Defence can -- the Defence is allowed not to notify immediately the fact that all details pertaining to the defence of alibi. Although according to me, it's obvious that the Defence explained and set out very clearly the defence of the alibi in question. And I repeat once again: It's the fact that Mr. Stankovic was not on the scene during 90 per cent of the time in question, and that when he went to the house, he went to the front of the house only, as part of the mission. This being said, I believe that we've completed the preparation of the case. I'm sorry, Mr. Wubben. You wanted to take the floor? Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It was not my purpose to interrupt you, but it was my purpose to clarify the position of the Prosecution in regard to your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, indeed, the Prosecution agreed that we are trial ready, with caveat of the 11 bis. But I would like to add another caveat to it, as it had been raised today. But first the caveat of the motion for 11 bis-ing. If this means that in the belief of Your Honour, it is so that you, as a Pre-Trial Judge, have separate power, and it is as such enshrined in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, then, related to that caveat, I have a request to you from the Prosecution team to see to it, in accordance with Rule 65 ter, that there is no undue delay, and I refer to 65 ter, under (B), meaning not an undue delay whenever it comes to preparing for trial, but whenever it comes to the fact that two Trial Chambers are now in charge of various aspects of this case. Whenever two Trial Chambers are operating in a separate, isolated way, without communicating or without a shared policy, then it will be counter-productive and there might be a delay that will in a disadvantage of a quick proceeding of the case. In that regard, with all respects to the powers and the fact that I acknowledge that you are the Pre-Trial Judge, at the same time, I ask you, in your position as Pre-Trial Judge, to set up communication in order to support a shared policy with a deciding in the case in such a manner that there will be either a deferral or a proceeding in an expeditious way, in an expeditious manner. Second caveat, Your Honour, is the aspect of the national laws and regulations by Bosnia and Herzegovina in respect to the laws of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and the Statute. It's the opinion of the Prosecution that Article 9 of the Statute and Rule 89 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence confirms that this Tribunal is independent and has primacy over national court and also is not bound by international laws, meaning that whenever there is a motion based upon 11 bis, that simple filing of such a motion doesn't change those Articles, the principle that it is the Statute and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence that rules this Court, and not being bound by any national proceedings, predicaments or principles as referred to by the Defence counsel, meaning also that the Prosecution believe that Article 67 should be met, and for the time being, I take it that whenever an alibi defence has been argued, then it should be fully argued in accordance with the Rules. Even if national laws point out in another direction, it should be so that an alibi argumentation should meet the specifications as confirmed in Rule 67, under (A), sub -- the first one, under the paragraph of the defence of alibi, referring to the place or places at which the accused claimed to have been present, and also the times of the alleged crime, and also the names and addresses of witnesses and other evidence upon which the accused intends to rely to establish the alibi. Those conditions have not been met, in my opinion. That's why I bring this now to your attention that it is the Prosecution's belief that, first, before we proceed further, those conditions should be met and should be implemented in clarification or a motion by the Defence counsel. So we have here two caveats by the Prosecution. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I will be in a position to answer very quickly, by saying the following: I make a clear distinction between bringing justice and the administration of justice. What I mean by that is that my duty is to fulfil the preparation of the case, to complete the preparation of the case. You know as well as I do that the Pre-Trial Judge, once the pre-trial preparation is over, has to prepare a report that is submitted to the Presiding Judge of the Trial Chamber, who then informs the President of the Tribunal of the fact. Here we are talking about the administration of justice. And this has nothing to do with serving justice, because the Pre-Trial Judge has a judicial function that is not charged with the administration of justice itself, for example, the politics of the Tribunal, the creation of -- the setting up of the Trial Chamber to rule on the 11 bis motion, for example. So here we are talking about two different areas that are distinct. My duty is to make sure that the preparation of the case goes ahead properly. Then the administration of justice will decide what to do with the report that I've submitted. If the case is ready for trial, why not try it here, here in the Tribunal? But it's not -- I have nothing to do with that. I have nothing to do with the administration of justice. I am -- I cannot wait for decisions, decisions that might be taken next week, next month, or next year. No one knows. You submitted a motion, but are you able to tell me when the ruling will be handed down? No, you can't. Therefore, we are dealing here with matters that are -- do not necessarily relate to one another. Therefore, I am here to fulfil my duty, I'm here to draw up my report. If we all agree that the case is ready for trial, then I'm supposed to draw up a report under the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and to submit it to the Tribunal, who will then make a decision. My duty is to make sure that the case is prepared properly. You said you had two caveats, first of all, there is this Rule 11 bis motion. The second point you had, if I understand correctly, has to do with Rule 67. And you tell us that the Defence said that it intended to invoke a defence of alibi, and what you tell us is that the Defence has not complied with the dispositions of Rule 67. The Defence says that the -- there is no obligation under the Rule. I mentioned the defence of alibi myself. I said that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence said that it told you where the accused was during that period of time and then you're in a position to make the necessary verifications. The reason why the Rule is drawn up the way it is is that the Prosecutor should not be left in the dark, because it's not acceptable for the Prosecutor to prepare its case and then for the accused to come and say: Well, I was not in the country. I was in hospital. I was being operated upon, et cetera. So the idea, the objective of the Rule is not to have the -- for the Prosecution not to be completely taken by surprise. But I think I explained the situation quite clearly. I believe that we can interpret the Rule in a slightly different manner, by saying: Yes, there is an obligation, but it is not necessarily automatic, i.e., when you invoke the defence of alibi, you do not have to immediately give the names of the witnesses, their addresses, and all relevant details mentioned in the Rule. And I'm saying that based on the French wording of the Rule 67 that says that the Defence notifies the Prosecutor, provides that information. I don't think that we can say that the Defence is trying to take the Prosecution by surprise, because the Defence has already interred the nature of the defence of alibi, because the Defence has said that Mr. Stankovic was not on the scene of the crimes; he was at the front; he was fighting; and that he never entered the house; and that when he went there, he was on a mission. So this is already the beginning of some information about the defence of alibi, and at this stage of the proceedings, in my opinion, that's enough. I do not mean to say that if a date is set for the beginning of the trial and if the Prosecution is set to present its case, then -- I'm not saying then it would -- then it would probably be appropriate for the Defence to disclose any other information about that matter. But I believe that the time has not come to demand from the Defence that they reveal all the information, and I don't think that this will prejudice the Prosecution. I do not think they will be prejudiced if they wait for a date to be set for the beginning of the trial before a Trial Chamber of the Tribunal. This was just a brief reply to your comments. Would you like to answer or to make any comments? I'm quite ready to listen to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour. But we will take it into consideration. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thanks. Mr. Radovic, you've listened to what I had to say. You've listened to the comments made by the Prosecution. Would you like to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The Defence maintains its position. You yourself have explained that. We believe that at this stage of the pre-trial proceedings, we do not have to submit any further motions detailing the defence of alibi of Mr. Stankovic. Another factor contributing to us not submitting that motion is something that I've already talked about. I would like to reiterate something else now. As I've said, from the moment when the Prosecution submitted its request pursuant to Rule 11 bis to have the case referred to a court in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I will refrain myself from taking any measures that might have negative repercussions on the proceedings that might take place against Mr. Stankovic in the war crimes court in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I will continue complying with all other obligations I have here before this Tribunal, as I have appeared here at a Status Conference today. In all other instances where I believe that Mr. Stankovic's right to a fair trial might be jeopardised, I will take action. Now, I have a question relating to the defence of Mr. Stankovic, which is this: What is going to happen if the case against Mr. Stankovic is referred to Bosnia and Herzegovina? Will Mr. Stankovic be in a position to make me accountable for the fact that I did not take action here, which is not compulsory action before the courts in Bosnia and Herzegovina, if these actions have an impact on his defence? In my opinion, there is a certain legal void in this issue, because this is a matter that has not been regulated by any Rule of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, especially not Rule 11 bis. What represents another problem for me is further disclosure of evidence. In view of the fact that parliamentary council and other chamber [as interpreted] in Bosnia and Herzegovina have not yet adopted all the laws that will regulate proceedings before the war crimes court in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I would like to know what weight will be accorded to the evidence gathered here at this Tribunal, because this might have repercussions on my obligation to continue with the disclosure of evidence to the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Radovic. So if I understand correctly, you are not opposed against completing the pre-trial stage, and I also understand that you want this case to be heard in this Tribunal. The last word goes to Mr. Stankovic. I will ask him to tell me if he has any complaints about his state of health. Mr. Stankovic, if you want us to go into private session, we can do so, and -- for you to be able to talk freely about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no need for that. But prior to that, I would like to make a correction so that we avoid any misunderstanding. Just a minute ago, when you spoke about my motion and quoted from it, you said that I did not spend 90 per cent of the time on the scene. This is not what I said or wrote. Because the scene is the house, the house in question, and that's not what I said. I said that I did not spend 90 per cent of my time in Miljevina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everyone understands properly, and I also stated that you only went to the house, and you never entered the house, but you only went to the house twice. That's clear enough, isn't it? Okay. You can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But you also stated that I did not spend 90 per cent of the time on the scene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. When I'm talking about the scene, it's not the house.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. All right. We understand each other now. Now I would like to say something else concerning the alibi. I cannot comprehend the Prosecution. They want to force us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Listen. Listen, Mr. Stankovic. I don't have any problems with that issue. I've made a decision. So there's no need to revisit the issue again. So would you like to inform me about -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- concerning my health?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, you are slowly and slyly destroying my health here. You have kept me here detained for three years without telling me what the charges are or when the trial would commence. That means that I need to spend some 20 years here under investigation; in the meantime, they are changing the indictment, bringing in new witnesses, taking out old witnesses. This is something I cannot comprehend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well. Well, well. So you do not have anything specific to say about that matter. Before concluding today's hearing, I would like to ask Mr. Radovic to make sure that any correspondence that is sent should comply with protective measures. And in the same vein, I would like to once again compliment and pay tribute to the Registry that reacted very appropriately and that made sure that no harm came from the infraction of protective measures. This being said, I think we've come to the end of this Status Conference. The hearing stands adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
